guide: OpenTTD Manual of Style (game, modelled on Microsoft guide)
rule: always put a title on an icon button; never put a title on a tooltip belonging to a button with text; "A tooltip without a title must always contain a description."
example: Build canals: Places a navigable waterway on flat land.

rule: "Spell out numbers from one to nine in descriptive texts by default"; never start a sentence with a numeral; numerals for measurement units, in-game values and amounts, percentages; related numbers in one text all numerals.

"Use sentence style capitalization by default"; title capitalisation for vehicle names, resources, currencies, locations, building names; "Don't use all uppercase for emphasis"; "UI labels will generally not form full sentences and never end with a period."; headings never end with punctuation.

guide: Battle for Wesnoth UI Style Guide (game)
rule: "Tooltips use sentence case, but the last sentence in any tooltip does not have a full stop." "Tooltips should contain no more than one or two lines of text." Phrase the tooltip to describe what happens when the option is turned on.
example: Auto-open whisper windows in lobby -> "When you are sent a whisper message, it appears in a pop-up window"

guide: Battle for Wesnoth UI Style Guide
rule: "Please avoid using 'OK' in favour of a specific word indicating what will happen when the button is clicked." Question gets a question mark; instruction is imperative and ends with a colon; information about what the computer is doing ends with an ellipsis.
example: Delete Game / "Do you really want to delete this game?"; Language / "Choose your preferred language:"

rule: "Do this to recover": say the fix, not the verdict. "To get what you want, do this": goal first, then action. "One sentence, one idea".
example: Do: "Shorten filename to 64 characters or less"; Don't: "Invalid filename". Do: "To save changes, drop a folder here"

rule: "Be friendly but not ridiculous"; "Cut, cut, cut" (please, sorry, very, awesome, there is); short synonyms; active voice; contractions; "Use sentence-case, not Title-Case"; "Don't spell out numbers".
example: Do: "DevTools loaded source maps"; Don't: "Source maps were loaded by DevTools". Do: "1, 2, 3"

rule: "explain what went wrong and how to fix it"; plain English, positive language; read aloud; be specific, not generic; avoid "please", "sorry", "valid/invalid", "oops"; instruction for empty fields, description for too-long entries.
example: Enter your first name / Name must be 35 characters or less / not "An error occurred", "This field is required"

guide: GOV.UK A to Z style guide
rule: "Write all other numbers in numerals (including 2 to 9)"; "Use '500 to 900' and not '500-900' (except in tables)"; "Avoid negative contractions like can't and don't"; "Don't use 'click' when talking about user interfaces... Use 'select'."; bold only for interface elements in instructions.

"When you write about numbers used in examples or UI, duplicate them exactly as they appear in the UI." Spell out zero to nine in body text but "It's OK to use numerals for zero through nine when you have limited space, such as in tables and UI." Numerals for measurements and percentages "no matter how small". Use en dash for ranges only where space is tight (tables, UI). "In UI, avoid the abbreviations [K, M, B] unless space is too limited"; "8.21K has the same number of characters as 8,210"; allow space for translation expansion.
example: 10 screen savers / five databases / At least 50 percent of your system resources

rule: Voice is constant; tone adapts "from serious to empathetic to lighthearted" to the customer's state of mind. "Get to the point fast. Start with the key takeaway... Make choices and next steps obvious." "Prune every excess word." Short everyday words, contractions, sentence-style capitalization.
example: Warm and relaxed / Crisp and clear / Ready to lend a hand

rule: "Instead of telling the user what they did wrong, tell the user how to get it right." "avoid the words 'sorry' or 'please'." "Don't attempt to make error messages humorous." "focus the error message on what went wrong rather than assigning blame."
example: Not: "You didn't enter a name." Do: "Enter a name." Not: "Is the server running? Better go catch it :D" Do: "The server is temporarily unavailable. Try again in a few minutes." Not: "You specified a printer that's offline." Do: "The specified printer is offline."

rule: "To refer to a button, use the button's label." "Don't use UI elements as if they were English verbs or nouns." Follow the page's capitalization; "Don't use directional language to orient the reader." Drop a trailing ellipsis from the name.
example: Do: "To save the settings, click Save." Not: "Save the settings." Do: "Click Browse." Not: "Click Browse ..."

rule: "Start button labels with a verb." "Aim for using one to two words, with a maximum of four words." Sentence case, no punctuation. "Don't use colons after labels." "Write error messages for humans without blame." Confirmations: "Use affirmative actions with verbs" and "explain the impact and consequences of the options".
example: Save changes (not Save Changes); Search by type (not Search by type:); "Use Google's location service?" over "Are you sure?"; "The server is unresponsive." over "Oops, the server appears to be on a break."

rule: "Mailchimp's tone is usually informal, but it's always more important to be clear than entertaining." "forced humor can be worse than none at all." "If you're unsure, keep a straight face." Match tone to whether the reader is "scared or upset" versus laughing. The page gives no error-message-specific rule.

topic: game text size, case, line width
rule: Minimum body height: console 26 px at 1080p, PC/VR 18 px at 1080p; players can scale to 200% "without losing content, functionality, or meaning"; scaling never forces two-axis scrolling; blocks over two lines: max line width 80 characters; "provide the ability to display text in sentence case rather than ALL CAPS or all lowercase" (one or two word labels exempt); text inside icons meets the same minimums.

guide: Wayline: UX writing for indie games
rule: "Prioritize clarity and conciseness"; keep one consistent voice; developers assume confusing text is "part of the charm" and the article calls that assumption dangerous. No in-world-vs-clarity rule given.
example: cryptic error messages vs "helpful and informative" ones (case study, no strings)

source: https://polaris.shopify.com/content/error-messages (redirects to shopify.dev, page no longer fetchable)
rule: Search-result summary only, unverified: buttons lead with a strong verb, verb+noun except common actions (Save, Close, Cancel, OK); errors name the effect on the merchant, give specifics, avoid 'invalid'; offer a one-click fix where possible.
example: Activate Apple Pay / View shipping settings, not Try Apple Pay (from snippet)

rule: Fetch returned only the page title (JS-rendered). Nothing quoted.
